Long-term intermittent treatment with inhaled antibacterials, particularly to- bramycin, is favoured;8,9,17,18 other nebulised antibacteri- als that may be of benefit include aztreonam and colis- tin.8,19 A systematic review confirmed that inhaled antipseudomonal antibacterials improved lung function and reduced the frequency of exacerbations.20 Although there is some evidence of an increase in resistance with such treatment,20 it is claimed to be less frequent than feared.8 In contrast, oral antipseudomonal therapy has not been conclusively shown to be of benefit in chronic infec- tion,21 and is generally avoided because of fears of resist- ance.8 The macrolide azithromycin is, however, used orally in chronic infection, but may be acting as an immunomodu- lator to reduce inflammation rather than specifically as an antibacterial.8,9,22 A systematic review23 on the use of macrolides in cystic fibrosis found evidence of a small but significant improvement in respiratory function at 6 months with azithromycin compared with placebo; the role of other macrolides was unclear. A small anti-inflam- matory benefit has also been reported from treatment with high-dose oral ibuprofen,24 and this is used in some cen- tres, particularly in the USA.9 However, there are some concerns about the potential for adverse effects; it has been recommended that if used, such therapy be stopped in pa- tients who require intravenous aminoglycosides, and should be avoided in those with gastrointestinal risk fac- tors.24 There is no evidence supporting a role for cortico- steroid therapy,25,26 except in the management of patients who develop allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.9 Aggressive management of exacerbations with appro- priate antibacterials is crucial.8,9,27,28 Treatment should be based on recent culture results, but there appears to be no additional value in combination antibacterial sensitivity testing.29 In patients with Ps. aeruginosa infection a com- bination of intravenous antibacterials, typically an aminoglycoside such as tobramycin and a beta-lactam with antipseudomonal activity such as ceftazidime, is fa- voured.27,28,30 Once-daily dosing with the aminoglycoside is as effective as giving it in divided doses, and may be associated with less nephrotoxicity in children.31 High doses are necessary because of the poor penetration of these antipseudomonal antibacterials into the site of infec- tion and their increased renal clearance in patients with cystic fibrosis.32,33 Treatment is generally given for 2 to 3 weeks although there is no good evidence to support a par- ticular length of therapy.34 Intermittent elective intrave- nous therapy has become more practical with the develop- ment of regimens that enable patients to be treated at home.30,
